questions.question: What is a method reference in Java 8 and why would you use it?
questions.title: What Is a Method Reference in Java 8?
questions.direct_answer: A method reference is shorthand syntax for a lambda expression that only calls an existing method. Instead of writing (x) -> obj.method(x), you write obj::method. It makes code cleaner when the lambda does nothing but delegate to a single method call.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that method references are syntactic sugar over lambdas and recognize when they improve readability.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking method references are a completely different feature from lambdas rather than just a more concise syntax for the same thing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the compiler converts method references to the same functional interface implementation as lambdas, so they have identical performance and behavior.

sections.title: Understanding Method References as Lambda Shorthand
sections.content:
A **method reference** is a shorthand for a lambda whose whole body is a single call to an existing method. Where a lambda spells out the parameter and the call, a method reference names the method directly with the `::` operator. For example, the lambda `s -> s.toUpperCase()` becomes `String::toUpperCase`.

Why it exists: when a lambda does nothing but forward its argument to one method, the parameter name is just noise. A method reference removes that noise so the code reads like plain **intent**.

How it works: the part before `::` is the target (a class or an object) and the part after is the method. The compiler still builds a **functional interface** implementation behind the scenes, exactly as it would for the equivalent lambda.

There are four shapes you will meet:
- `Math::max` — a static method reference
- `System.out::println` — bound to a specific object
- `String::toUpperCase` — unbound, where the argument becomes the receiver
- `ArrayList::new` — a constructor reference

> **The gotcha:** a method reference and its lambda compile to identical bytecode, so the choice is purely about readability — never performance.

sections.title: Method Reference at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Method reference|~shorthand for a lambda|Class::method syntax|calls an existing method|since Java 8
blue|When|~lambda just calls one method|x -> obj.m(x)|becomes obj::m|no new logic added
emerald|Wins|~less noise|reuses a named method|reads like intent|works anywhere a lambda does

sections.title: Lambda that only forwards its argument
Method reference: same behavior, less noise
sections.content:
```java
List<String> names = List.of("amy", "bob");

names.forEach(System.out::println);                 // bound instance ref
names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase).toList();   // unbound instance ref
```

*Switch to a method reference only when the lambda forwards its arguments unchanged.*

sections.title: Method Reference vs Lambda Comparison
When Method References Make Sense
sections.content: Use method references when your lambda body contains **exactly one method call** with no additional logic or transformations. They shine in **stream pipelines** where you're chaining operations like filtering, mapping, and collecting—for example, **employees.stream().map(Employee::getSalary).filter(Objects::nonNull)** is far more readable than the lambda equivalent. Method references are particularly valuable in **Spring applications** where you pass repository methods as callbacks, like **userRepository.findAll().forEach(emailService::sendWelcome)**. If you need to add any logic (checking conditions, transforming arguments, calling multiple methods), stick with a lambda. The readability test is simple: if the method reference makes someone pause to understand what's happening, the lambda was probably clearer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating them as different from lambdas**: Freshers often think method references are a separate feature with different semantics, but they're literally just shorter syntax for single-method lambdas—the compiler generates identical code.
- **Forcing method references everywhere**: Just because your IDE suggests converting a lambda to a method reference doesn't mean you should—if **(x) -> service.process(x, DEFAULT_MODE)** is clearer than creating a wrapper method just to use a reference, keep the lambda.
- **Mismatching signatures**: Writing **list.forEach(this::print)** when **print()** takes two parameters but forEach supplies only one will cause a compilation error—the method signature must exactly match what the functional interface expects.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Syntactic sugar**: Method references compile to the same bytecode as equivalent lambdas with identical runtime performance
- **Double colon operator**: The :: syntax separates the target (class or object) from the method name being referenced
- **Functional interface match**: The referenced method's signature must match the abstract method of the target functional interface
- **Readability guideline**: Use method references when they make intent clearer, not just because they're shorter
- **Zero overhead**: No additional object creation or indirection—method references are as efficient as lambdas
- **IDE support**: Modern IDEs highlight conversion opportunities but prioritize clarity over mechanical refactoring
- **Stream compatibility**: Method references work seamlessly with Stream API operations like map, filter, and forEach

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A method reference is a shorter way to write a lambda when the lambda just calls one existing method. Instead of writing something like x goes to x dot length, you'd write String colon colon length. They use the double colon operator to reference the method. The reason you'd use them is purely readability. When you're working with streams or functional interfaces, your code gets cleaner because you're not repeating the obvious parameter passing. For example, in a stream pipeline, names dot stream dot map with String colon colon toUpperCase is easier to read than names dot stream dot map with a lambda that takes s and returns s dot toUpperCase. It's the same thing under the hood though. The compiler converts both to the exact same bytecode, so there's no performance difference at all. One thing to watch out for is that the method signature has to match what the functional interface expects. If you're using forEach which takes a Consumer with one parameter, you can't reference a method that needs two parameters. That won't compile. The best advice is to use method references when they make your intent clearer to someone reading the code, not just because they're shorter. Sometimes a lambda with an explicit parameter name actually explains what's happening better, especially if the transformation isn't obvious.

questions.question: When should you use a method reference instead of a lambda in Java?
questions.title: Method Reference vs Lambda: When to Use Which
questions.direct_answer: Use a method reference when the lambda body does nothing except call one existing method with no transformations. Use a lambda when you need to add any logic, call multiple methods, or transform arguments before passing them. Readability is the deciding factor—choose whichever form makes the intent clearer to someone reading your code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment—can you make context-dependent decisions rather than mechanically applying rules without thinking.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing method references everywhere just because they're shorter, even when a lambda would be clearer or when the reference obscures intent.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that IDE suggestions to convert lambdas to method references are helpful hints, not strict rules—prioritize code clarity over mechanical refactoring.

sections.title: Balancing Brevity with Clarity
sections.content:
Both a **lambda** and a **method reference** create an instance of a functional interface. The difference is only in how much you write. A lambda spells out the parameters and the body, while a method reference names an existing method with the `::` operator and lets the compiler wire up the rest.

The rule of thumb is simple. Reach for a method reference when the lambda body is exactly one call that forwards its arguments untouched. Keep the lambda the moment any real work appears.

- Pure forwarding like `x -> repo.save(x)` becomes `repo::save`.
- Extra logic like `x -> service.process(x, true)` has to stay a lambda.
- Chained calls like `s -> s.trim().toLowerCase()` have no single method to point at.

**Readability** is the deciding factor, not brevity for its own sake. If a method reference makes a reader pause, the lambda was the clearer choice.

> **The gotcha:** an IDE suggestion to convert a lambda is a hint, not a rule — sometimes the named parameter explained the intent better.

sections.title: Method Reference vs Lambda
sections.content:
amber|Method reference|~lambda only forwards args|same argument order|no extra logic|Class::method
blue|Keep the lambda|~reorders or transforms args|adds a condition|multiple statements|x -> f(x) + 1
emerald|Rule|~pure forwarding -> reference|any real work -> lambda|readability first|don't force it

sections.title: When a method reference fits vs when to keep the lambda
Step 1: Check Lambda Body Complexity
sections.content: First, examine what happens inside the lambda body. If it's **one method call** where parameters pass through directly with no changes—like **(x) -> repository.save(x)** which becomes **repository::save**—a method reference is cleaner. If you're doing **anything extra** like adding default values **(x) -> service.process(x, true)**, checking conditions **(x) -> x != null ? x.trim() : "")**, or chaining multiple operations **(x) -> x.toUpperCase().trim()**, keep the lambda. The transformation effort matters: creating a helper method just to satisfy method reference syntax usually makes code harder to follow, not easier.

sections.title: Step 2: Evaluate Reader Context and Intent
sections.content: Second, consider who's reading this code and whether the method reference makes your **intent obvious**. In stream pipelines with standard operations, method references are idiomatic—**employees.stream().filter(Objects::nonNull).map(Employee::getName)** reads naturally to any Java developer. But for domain-specific methods, explicit lambdas can clarify **what's being extracted** or **why you're filtering**: **(order) -> order.getTotal() > 1000** explains the business rule better than extracting an **Order::isHighValue** method just to use a reference. When the method name is self-documenting like **String::trim**, use the reference. When the logic needs context like **employee -> calculateTax(employee, currentYear, region)**, the lambda provides that context inline.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Blindly accepting IDE suggestions**: IntelliJ and Eclipse suggest converting lambdas to method references mechanically, but freshers often click "Accept" without considering whether it actually improves readability—sometimes the lambda's parameter name provided useful context.
- **Creating wrapper methods unnecessarily**: Writing a helper method **private void sendEmail(User u) { emailService.send(u.getEmail()); }** just so you can write **users.forEach(this::sendEmail)** instead of **users.forEach(u -> emailService.send(u.getEmail()))** adds indirection without value.
- **Overusing bound references in loops**: Capturing **this::processItem** inside a loop where the captured state changes per iteration creates subtle bugs because the reference captures the binding at creation time, not invocation time.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Single method call rule**: Method references only make sense when the lambda body contains exactly one method invocation with direct parameter passing
- **No transformation allowed**: The moment you need to modify arguments, add defaults, or check conditions, a lambda is required
- **Readability over brevity**: Shorter isn't always better—choose the form that makes intent clearest to future readers
- **IDE hints not rules**: Automated suggestions to convert lambdas are helpful pointers but shouldn't override human judgment about clarity
- **Domain context matters**: Standard library methods like String::trim are universally clear, but custom business methods may need lambda context
- **Avoid wrapper methods**: Don't create helper methods solely to satisfy method reference syntax if the lambda was already clear
- **Stream idioms**: Method references are particularly idiomatic in stream pipelines where operations chain naturally

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You should use a method reference when your lambda is doing nothing except calling one existing method, and the parameters pass through directly without any changes. That's the key test. If you've got something like x goes to repository dot save of x, just write repository colon colon save instead. It's cleaner and the intent is obvious. But the moment you need to add any logic, stick with the lambda. For example, if you're doing x goes to service dot process of x comma true because you're passing a default flag, you can't use a method reference there. You'd have to create a wrapper method just to satisfy the syntax, and that's usually not worth it. Readability is the real deciding factor. If the method reference makes your code easier to understand, use it. If it obscures what's happening, keep the lambda. A common scenario is stream pipelines. Something like employees dot stream dot map with Employee colon colon getName is completely natural because every Java developer recognizes that pattern. But for domain-specific logic, sometimes the lambda is clearer because the parameter name gives context. Like employee goes to employee dot getSalary times bonus rate—seeing that inline helps you understand the calculation. Don't feel pressured to use method references everywhere just because your IDE suggests it. Those are helpful hints, not rules. I'd prioritize making the code clear to someone who's reading it six months from now over mechanically shortening every lambda.

questions.question: How do you use method references with Comparator.comparing() for sorting?
questions.title: Sorting with Comparator.comparing() and Method References
questions.direct_answer: Use Comparator.comparing() with a method reference to extract the field you want to sort by. For example, list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)) sorts by name. You can chain thenComparing() for multi-field sorting and call reversed() for descending order. It's cleaner than writing manual compare logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java 8 API knowledge—can you use method references with real library methods like Comparator in everyday sorting scenarios.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing manual lambda comparators like (a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName()) when Comparator.comparing with a method reference is built for exactly this case.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show multi-field sorting with thenComparing and mention reversed for descending order, demonstrating fluent API knowledge beyond basic usage.

sections.title: Modern Sorting with Comparator and Method References
sections.content:
**`Comparator.comparing()`** builds a comparator from a key extractor—a function that pulls the field you want to sort by out of each object. Pass it a method reference and the sort definition reads almost like English. Instead of hand-writing `(a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName())`, you write `Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)`.

Why it helps: the boilerplate of null checks and manual `compareTo` calls disappears, and the **intent**—sort by name—sits right there in the code.

The API is **fluent**, so comparators chain:
- `reversed()` flips ascending into descending.
- `thenComparing()` adds a tie-breaker on a second field.
- `nullsLast()` and `nullsFirst()` decide where missing values land.

Under the hood `Person::getName` is an unbound reference, so each element in the list becomes the receiver of `getName()` when the comparator runs.

> **The gotcha:** `reversed()` must be called on the comparator instance, not stacked before `comparing()`.

sections.title: Sorting with Comparator.comparing
sections.content:
amber|comparing(key)|~sort by an extracted key|User::getAge|method-reference key|natural order
blue|Chain|~thenComparing(...)|tie-breakers|multi-field sort|stable ordering
emerald|Modifiers|~reversed()|nullsFirst / nullsLast|comparingInt for primitives|avoids boxing

sections.title: Sorting with Comparator.comparing and Method References
When to Use Comparator.comparing with Method References
sections.content:
Use this pattern whenever you're sorting **collections or streams** by object properties—it's the modern standard in Java codebases. It shines in **REST API responses** where you need to sort database results before returning them: **orders.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Order::getCreatedDate).reversed())** gives you most recent first.

Use **thenComparing()** for **multi-level sorting** like leaderboards where you sort by score descending, then by completion time ascending: **Comparator.comparing(Player::getScore).reversed().thenComparing(Player::getTime)**. The null-handling methods **nullsFirst()** and **nullsLast()** are essential when sorting data from external sources that might have missing values—without them, you risk NullPointerException. For **custom comparison logic** beyond simple property extraction (like case-insensitive string sorting), combine with **Comparator.comparing(Person::getName, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing manual comparators**: Freshers often write **(a, b) -> a.getName().compareTo(b.getName())** instead of **Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)**, missing that the library method handles null safety and cleaner syntax.
- **Reversed placement confusion**: Writing **Comparator.reversed().comparing(Employee::salary)** instead of **Comparator.comparing(Employee::salary).reversed()**—reversed() must be called on the Comparator instance, not the static method.
- **Ignoring null values**: Using **Comparator.comparing(Employee::getManager)** on objects where manager can be null causes NullPointerException—wrap with **Comparator.comparing(Employee::getManager, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))** or filter nulls first.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Key extractor pattern**: Comparator.comparing() takes a function that extracts the property to compare, typically a method reference
- **Fluent chaining**: thenComparing() adds secondary sort criteria, applied when the primary comparison yields equality
- **Reversed order**: Call reversed() on any Comparator instance to flip ascending to descending sort order
- **Null safety**: Use nullsFirst() or nullsLast() to handle null values explicitly rather than letting them cause exceptions
- **Custom comparators**: Second parameter to comparing() accepts a custom Comparator like String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER
- **Stream integration**: Works seamlessly with Stream.sorted() for inline sorting during stream processing
- **Immutable patterns**: Returns new sorted lists when using streams with toList() or collect(), leaving original data unchanged

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You use method references with Comparator dot comparing to make sorting cleaner and more readable. The basic pattern is Comparator dot comparing and you pass a method reference that extracts the field you want to sort by. So if you've got a list of Person objects and you want to sort by name, you'd write list dot sort with Comparator dot comparing Person colon colon getName. That extracts the name from each person and compares them alphabetically. What makes this powerful is the fluent API. You can chain then comparing for multi-field sorting. For example, if you want to sort by department first, then by salary within each department, you'd write Comparator dot comparing Employee colon colon department dot then comparing Employee colon colon salary. The order matters—it sorts by the first criterion, and only uses the second when the first comparison is equal. For descending order, call reversed on the comparator. So Comparator dot comparing Employee colon colon salary dot reversed gives you highest salary first. You can also apply reversed to just one field in a multi-field sort by passing Comparator dot reverse order as the second argument to then comparing. One thing that trips up freshers is null handling. If your field might be null, you need to wrap it with nulls last or nulls first. Otherwise you'll get a NullPointerException when it tries to compare. This pattern is way better than writing manual comparison logic like a comma b goes to a dot get name dot compare to b dot get name. It's shorter, less error-prone, and reads more naturally.

questions.question: What are the four types of method references in Java 8? Give an example of each.
questions.title: Four Types of Method References in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: The four types are: static method reference (Math::max), bound instance method reference (str::length using a specific object), unbound instance method reference (String::toUpperCase where the instance comes from the context), and constructor reference (ArrayList::new). Each serves a different use case depending on whether you're calling a static method, instance method on a known object, instance method on a parameter, or a constructor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can categorize method references correctly and understand the subtle difference between bound and unbound instance method references.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing bound versus unbound instance references—bound uses a specific object instance captured from the enclosing scope, while unbound treats the first parameter as the receiver object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that unbound instance method references are especially useful with streams, where each element becomes the receiver of the method call.

sections.title: Four Categories of Method References
sections.content:
A **method reference** points at a method that already exists, using the `::` operator, so a lambda that only calls that method can be written more directly. Java 8 sorts these references into **four types**, and the split comes down to one question: where does the object that the method runs on come from?

- **Static** — `Integer::parseInt`. There's no object at all; the class owns the method.
- **Bound instance** — `System.out::println`. A specific object is captured now, and every call runs on it.
- **Unbound instance** — `String::toUpperCase`. There's no object yet; the first argument becomes the receiver, which is why streams love this form.
- **Constructor** — `ArrayList::new`. The reference builds a new object instead of calling a method.

The compiler picks the matching shape from the target **functional interface**, so the same `::` syntax quietly does four different jobs.

> **The gotcha:** bound and unbound look almost identical, but a variable before `::` means bound, while a class name means unbound.

sections.title: The Four Method Reference Types
sections.content:
amber|Static|~ClassName::staticMethod|Integer::parseInt|no instance needed|args passed through
blue|Bound instance|~object::method|System.out::println|a fixed receiver|object captured
emerald|Unbound instance|~ClassName::instanceMethod|String::toUpperCase|first arg is the receiver|one per element
violet|Constructor|~ClassName::new|ArrayList::new|acts as Supplier / Function|a factory reference

sections.title: All Four Method Reference Types in Action
Choosing the Right Method Reference Type
sections.content:
Use **static method references** when you need utility functions like **Math::abs**, **Integer::parseInt**, or **Collections::sort** that don't depend on instance state.

Use **bound instance method references** when you have a specific object captured in your scope and want to call its method repeatedly—common in **event handlers** like **button.setOnAction(logger::logEvent)** where logger is a field.

Use **unbound instance method references** in **stream pipelines** where each element needs to call its own method—**employees.stream().map(Employee::getSalary)** is the canonical example because each Employee object becomes the receiver.

Use **constructor references** when you need **factory patterns** or **Supplier implementations**, especially with **Stream.collect()** like **stream.collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new))**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing bound vs unbound**: Freshers write **String::length** thinking it will call length on a specific string they have in scope, but that's wrong—it's unbound so it expects the string as a parameter. For a specific string object like myStr, you'd need **myStr::length** (bound).
- **Wrong parameter count**: Using **employees.stream().map(Employee::calculateBonus)** when calculateBonus takes a parameter won't compile—the method signature must match the functional interface exactly.
- **Null captured objects**: With bound references like **user::getEmail**, if user is null when the reference is created, you'll get NullPointerException when the reference executes, not when you write the reference syntax.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Static references**: ClassName::staticMethod for class-level utility methods that don't need instance state
- **Bound instance**: object::method captures a specific object from enclosing scope, calls method on that same object every time
- **Unbound instance**: ClassName::instanceMethod where the functional interface's first parameter becomes the receiver object
- **Constructor references**: ClassName::new treated as factory—parameter count determines which constructor overload gets called
- **Stream pipeline context**: Unbound references dominate in streams because each element flows through as the receiver
- **Capture timing**: Bound references capture the object when the reference is created, not when it executes
- **Signature matching**: The method's parameter list and return type must exactly match the target functional interface

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are four types of method references in Java 8. First is the static method reference using ClassName colon colon methodName, like Math colon colon max. This calls a static method on a class. Second is the bound instance method reference where you have a specific object and you write object colon colon method. For example, if I have a String called myString, I can write myString colon colon length, and it'll always call length on that exact string object. Third is the unbound instance method reference, which looks like ClassName colon colon instanceMethod, such as String colon colon toUpperCase. The key difference from bound is that here you don't have a specific object yet—the object comes from the functional interface parameter. This is super common in streams. When you write names dot stream dot map with String colon colon toUpperCase, each name string in the stream becomes the object that toUpperCase gets called on. Fourth is the constructor reference using ClassName colon colon new, like ArrayList colon colon new. This creates new instances and is useful for factory patterns. The tricky part for freshers is telling apart bound and unbound instance references. If you see a variable name before the colon colon, that's bound—it's calling the method on that specific object. If you see a class name, that's unbound, and the object will come from the parameter. This matters a lot in streams where you want each element to be the receiver.

questions.question: What is a constructor reference in Java 8 and when would you use it?
questions.title: Constructor References in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A constructor reference uses ClassName::new syntax to reference a constructor as a functional interface. It's used when you need a factory or supplier that creates instances—for example, Supplier<User> factory = User::new creates a User with the no-arg constructor, or Function<String, User> factory = User::new with a single-argument constructor. The functional interface signature must match the constructor's parameter list.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all four method reference types including constructor references, which are less intuitive than the others.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognizing that the functional interface's parameter types must exactly match the constructor signature for the reference to compile.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate a factory pattern example using constructor references, showing how they enable flexible object creation without explicit new keywords scattered throughout code.

sections.title: Constructor References as Factory Abstractions
sections.content:
A **constructor reference** uses the `ClassName::new` syntax to treat a constructor as if it were a method you can pass around. Wherever a functional interface expects something that produces an object, a constructor reference fits in place of a lambda like `() -> new ArrayList<>()`.

Why it's useful: it turns object creation into a value. Instead of scattering `new` calls through the code, you hand `User::new` to whatever needs to build users, and that code stays generic.

The **functional interface** decides which constructor runs, based on parameter count and types:
- `Supplier<User>` with `User::new` calls the no-arg constructor.
- `Function<String, User>` with `User::new` calls the one-String constructor.
- `String[]::new` builds a correctly typed array for `Stream.toArray()`.

> **The gotcha:** if no constructor matches the interface's signature, `User::new` simply won't compile — the match is checked at compile time, not at runtime.

sections.title: Constructor References in Factory Patterns
When Constructor References Provide Value
sections.content:
Use constructor references in **factory method patterns** where you want to decouple object creation from the code that uses the objects—pass **User::new** to a service that creates users based on external data without that service needing to know User's constructor details. They're essential in **Stream.collect()** with **Collectors.toCollection()** when you need a specific collection implementation: **stream.collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new))** preserves insertion order while eliminating duplicates. Constructor references shine in **dependency injection** scenarios where you configure object creation once: **BeanFactory.register("user", User::new)** lets the framework handle instantiation.

Use **array constructor references** like **String[]::new** with **Stream.toArray()** to specify the array type you want back. They're particularly useful in **generic factory interfaces** where you want compile-time type safety: **Repository<User> repo = new Repository<>(User::new)** ensures the repository creates the correct type.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Signature mismatch**: Using **Supplier<User>** with **User::new** when User has no no-arg constructor causes compilation failure—the functional interface parameter count must exactly match an available constructor.
- **Ambiguous constructors**: If a class has multiple constructors with the same parameter count but different types (like User(String name) and User(Integer id)), the compiler can't resolve **User::new** without more type context—you may need an explicit lambda instead.
- **Forgetting array type**: Writing **stream.toArray()** returns Object array, but freshers expect their element type—you must use the array constructor reference like **stream.toArray(String[]::new)** to get the correct array type back.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ClassName::new syntax**: References a constructor, the specific overload determined by functional interface signature
- **Functional interface matching**: Parameter types and count of the interface's abstract method select which constructor overload gets invoked
- **Supplier for no-arg**: Supplier functional interface works with no-arg constructors to create instances on demand
- **Function for single-arg**: Function<InputType, OutputType> references single-parameter constructors for transformation operations
- **Collection factory pattern**: Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new) specifies collection implementation without hardcoding instantiation
- **Array constructor**: Type[]::new syntax in Stream.toArray() creates correctly-typed arrays instead of Object arrays
- **Decoupling creation**: Constructor references separate object creation logic from usage code, improving testability and flexibility

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A constructor reference in Java 8 uses the ClassName colon colon new syntax to reference a constructor as if it were a method. It lets you pass object creation logic around as a functional interface instead of explicitly calling new every time you need an instance. The functional interface you're using determines which constructor overload gets called. If you use Supplier with User colon colon new, that calls the no-arg constructor because Supplier has no parameters. If you use Function with String comma User and User colon colon new, it calls the constructor that takes one String parameter. The main use case is factory patterns. Instead of scattering new User calls throughout your code, you can pass User colon colon new to methods that need to create users. This makes your code more flexible because you can swap out the implementation by changing the constructor reference without touching all the places that use it. A really common practical example is with Stream dot collect. When you want a specific collection type, you write stream dot collect with Collectors dot to collection and pass the constructor reference like TreeSet colon colon new. That tells the collector what type of collection to create for storing the results. Another place you see this is array creation with streams. If you write stream dot to array without arguments, you get an Object array. But if you pass String array colon colon new, you get back a properly typed String array. The key thing to remember is that the parameter types and count of your functional interface have to exactly match one of the class's constructors. If there's no matching constructor, it won't compile. This is one of those features that feels weird at first but becomes really natural once you start using it in real code.
